Reviewer guide · Math Level 4

Thank you for helping again. Math Level 4 of LearnGED is now complete: 24 lessons and 24 practice pages, in English and in Spanish. With it, the four Math levels are done. Level 4 is the last step before the GED math test: the coordinate plane and the equation of a line, volume of spheres, cones, and pyramids, polynomials and factoring, quadratic equations, rational expressions, systems of equations and inequalities, and functions (linear, quadratic, and exponential).

A level is marked 🟢 ready only after a GED teacher who teaches in English has reviewed it. The Level 3 guide explains the conventions shared by Levels 3 and 4; this guide focuses on what is new in Level 4.

1. What to review

Each lesson is the main page (about 4 hours of student work). Its practice page has 3 to 6 activities that make new exercises every time; the lesson links to each one. The Spanish column is there only if you want to compare: both versions are built from the same source, so they must teach exactly the same thing.

2. How to split the work

Nobody needs to read all 48 pages. Two ways that work well:

  • By topic: each reviewer takes one or two topics (3 lessons each) and signs off on them in section 9.
  • By sample: if you have only an hour, read one lesson and its practice page all the way through, and skim the rest of that topic. Good samples: 1.2 (slope), 1.3 (equations of a line), 3.3 (factoring trinomials), 4.3 (quadratic formula), 6.1 (systems by substitution), 7.1 (graphing inequalities), 7.2 (functions), and 8.1 (the parabola).

In each lesson, please try the 8-question quiz at the end, and in each practice page do at least two exercises per activity, including one with a wrong answer on purpose, to see the hint.

↑ Back to top

3. What is new in Level 4

  • An interactive coordinate plane. The student marks points with the mouse, a finger, or the arrow keys, and drags points to see the slope and the line change.
  • Graphs drawn by the page. Lines, systems, solution regions of inequalities, parabolas, and exponential curves are drawn in the browser, with labels placed away from the axes and from the other lines.
  • Step by step. Most activities start with a “step by step” block that shows one move at a time before the student tries alone.
  • Answer checking for algebra. The pages read polynomials (3x^2 − 2x + 5), factored forms (2(x + 5)(x − 5)), ordered pairs, and solutions such as x = −3 or x = 5. They check that a factorization is correct and complete.
  • Feedback for systems. If a student's ordered pair is wrong, the page says whether it fits one equation but not the other.
  • Final project and final check (see above), and a review of the whole level in Lesson 8.3.
↑ Back to top

4. What to look for

  • Reading level. The algebra is harder here, but the sentences should not be. Mark any word or sentence that is too hard.
  • Tone. Our students are adults. Does anything sound childish, or too academic?
  • Math accuracy. Numbers, signs, rounding, units, and every step of the worked examples.
  • US usage. Anything that sounds translated or “not how we say it here” (see the questions in section 8).
  • Hints. Do the hints name the likely mistake without giving the answer away?
  • Answer checking. If you type a correct answer in another reasonable form and the page rejects it, please tell us what you typed.
  • Figures and graphs. Labels that overlap a line or a number on an axis, points in the wrong place, colors that are hard to tell apart.
  • Accessibility. Try the pages on a phone and with the keyboard only (the interactive graphs work with the arrow keys too).
↑ Back to top

5. How feedback works

The same idea as in Levels 1 and 2: a mistake is information, not a failure.

  1. First wrong answer: a hint that points to the specific mistake (for example, “Your point fits the first equation but not the second: check the substitution.”). The student tries again.
  2. Second wrong answer: the solution, explained step by step.
  3. Questions with only two choices (for example, “solid line or dashed line?”) show the explanation right away, because a second try would be a guess.
  4. Praise is about the strategy, not about being smart.

6. Math conventions

TopicLearnGED
Ordered pairs(x, y), with the x-coordinate first.
Distance and midpointd = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²) and M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). Negative coordinates go in parentheses when substituted.
Slopem = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁): “rise over run”. A horizontal line has slope 0; a vertical line has undefined slope.
Equation of a lineSlope-intercept y = mx + b, point-slope y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), and standard form Ax + By = C. Parallel lines have the same slope; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
Volume and surface areaThe formulas of the GED formula sheet. π answers as 36π or as a decimal (with the calculator's π key or 3.14). US units: inches, feet, cubic feet, gallons.
PolynomialsStandard form, highest degree first. Students type exponents with ^ (3x^2).
MultiplyingFOIL for two binomials, plus the special products (a + b)², (a − b)², and (a + b)(a − b).
FactoringAlways the greatest common factor first, then difference of squares or trinomials; the ac method when a ≠ 1. The answer must be factored completely.
Quadratic equationsSolved by factoring, by completing the square, or with the quadratic formula. Solutions such as x = −3 or x = 5; rounded answers to the hundredth are accepted.
Rational expressionsFactor, then cancel factors (never terms). Excluded values are stated: x ≠ 2.
SystemsSolution as an ordered pair. Three kinds: one solution, no solution, infinitely many solutions.
Inequalities in two variablesSolid line for ≤ and ≥, dashed line for < and >; a test point (usually (0, 0)) tells which side to shade. Only the solution region is shaded.
Functionsf(x) notation, domain and range, the vertical line test, and average rate of change = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).
Quadratic and exponential modelsVertex at x = −b/(2a). Exponential y = a · bˣ (growth if b > 1, decay if 0 < b < 1). Compound interest A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), money rounded to the cent. Heights in feet, distances in miles.

8. Questions for you

  1. Standard form. We write Ax + By = C, with whole numbers and A positive. Is that the form your students know?
  2. FOIL. Do you teach FOIL, or do you prefer the distributive property or the box (area) method only?
  3. Factoring trinomials with a ≠ 1. We teach the ac method. Do your students know another method (trial and error, the box method)?
  4. Completing the square (Lesson 4.2) is rarely needed on the GED. Is it worth keeping as the bridge to the quadratic formula?
  5. Compound interest and logarithms (Lesson 8.2) are not on the GED formula sheet. Should we keep them as enrichment?
  6. Rational expressions (Topic 5): is the depth right for GED students, or too much?
  7. Graphs. Are the graphs easy to read on a phone? Is anything too small?
  8. Final check. 30 questions, passing score 21 (70%). Is that a fair signal that a student is ready for the GED math test?

10. How to send comments

Any format is fine: an email, a list, or a screenshot with notes. Please say which page, which section (sections and activities are numbered), and, for exercises, what you typed: the practice exercises change every time, so a screenshot helps a lot. Send your comments to José M. Fernández (Zhema).

If you also teach science, social studies, or reading and writing, the page What comes next shows the plan for those subjects, and your ideas are welcome there too.
